newsitem.title: GERMANY: German report sees growth on track, jobless surge.
newsitem.headline: German report sees growth on track, jobless surge.

text.p: Germany's economy is expected to grow by 2.5 percent this year, up from 1.4 percent in 1996, according to an annual government economic report, details of which were obtained by Reuters on Tuesday.
Other key forecasts from the report include inflation at 1.5 percent, down from 1.8 percent, and a big jump in the unemployment rate to 11 percent from 10.3 percent last year.
Forecast figures were rounded to the nearest half point.

The report, which is still being drafted, shows Bonn is sticking to the growth forecast underpinning Finance Minister Theo Waigel's bid to cut state borrowing and qualify for European monetary union (EMU) this year.

Some independent economists expect gross domestic product to grow more slowly, pressuring tax revenues and making it harder to cut the budget deficit below the Maastricht treaty ceiling of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).

But the unemployment forecast represents a dramatic jump from independent forecasts made last autumn. Then, the six research institutes on whose forecasts Waigel based his 1997 budget, forecast the 1997 jobless rate at 10.4 percent.

Expressed in hard numbers, dole queues are seen averaging 4.2 million -- well over 200,000 higher than the view on which the budget was based. Officials and economists expect unemployment to hit a post-war record 4.5 million this winter.
The report, compiled by the Economics Ministry, is not due for publication until January 28. But the data are likely to pile the pressure on Waigel to slap a freeze on spending.

The Handelsblatt financial daily said last week that slower tax revenues could cost state coffers two billion marks ($1.23 billion) in lost revenues, while higher unemployment benefit payouts would add a further six billion marks to outgoings.

The Finance Ministry said last week that no decision had been taken on such a spending clampdown after borrowing overshot targets last year. Germany's public sector deficit was 3.9 percent of GDP in 1996, final data showed.
The report said the economies of both eastern and western Germany would grow at the same pace this year.
Private consumption was seen growing by 1.5 percent, just up from 1.4 percent last year. Industry investment was expected to turn around and rise by 1.5 percent after falling by 0.7 percent in 1996.

The main engine of recovery will continue to be exports, forecast to grow at 6.5 percent after 4.6 percent last year. Imports were seen expanding more slowly at 4.5 percent, up from two percent. ($1=1.6223 Mark)
